title: aham brahmasmi
tomorrow: the first feeling in the story isn't joy. what is it?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the four mahavakyas' first saying, prajnanam brahma, with a last word said twice. Today a new saying begins, in a new Upanishad, the Brihadaranyaka.

Somebody knocks. Who is it? And almost nobody answers with a name. It's me. The name comes second, if it comes at all. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad noticed that habit at the door, and its explanation starts before anything existed. The self is alone, in the shape of a person. It looks around and sees nothing but itself. And then, for the first time ever, it speaks.
screen: `WHO IS IT? IT'S ME.` → `THE SELF, ALONE.` → `NOTHING BUT ITSELF.` → `THEN IT SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: The first thing it says, the text tells us, is: I am. Aham asmi. And so, the story says, it came to be called I. Then the Upanishad steps out of the beginning and into an ordinary doorway. That's why, even now, when someone is called, they first answer, it's I, and only after that give whatever other name they have. Look at the order. I comes first. Every other name comes after: a family name, a nickname, a major, someone's daughter, someone's dad. They're real, and they matter. In this story they're added on. Now the saying this week is named for. A few verses later, the same chapter says that in the beginning this was Brahman, and it knew itself only: aham brahmasmi. I am Brahman. Aham, the very first word of the story, is the first word of the saying. So the great saying doesn't start up in the sky and work its way down to a person. It starts where the self in the story started, and where every answer at a door starts. With I. What the saying adds is a claim about what that plain I finally is.
screen: `THE FIRST WORD: I AM.` · `IT'S ME, THEN THE NAME.` · `EVERY OTHER NAME IS ADDED ON.` · `AHAM: THE STORY'S WORD, THE SAYING'S WORD.` · then, large: `I AM BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Say your own name once, quietly, out loud. Then say just: I am. Notice the difference: the name has a history, a family, a spelling; the I am is plainer, and in the story it came first. Rest with the plain one, saying it once more whenever the mind wanders off.
Aham brahmasmi: I am Brahman, the great saying of the Brihadaranyaka. Today's piece of it is the first word, aham: I.
Here's one to keep: aham brahmasmi, where every name you have comes after the I. See you tomorrow.
